title: Roots and Rational Exponents
presenterNotes: Students often confuse when to use ±. Emphasize: odd index → one root; even index, positive radicand → two roots (principal and negative).
When evaluating rational exponents, remind them they can take the root first or the power first. The root-first method usually yields smaller numbers.
For calculator use, stress the need for parentheses around fractional exponents to avoid order-of-operations errors.
The depreciation formula is a great real-world application. Walk through each variable carefully, and show that (S/C)^(1/n) is an nth root.

examples.title: Example C — Odd Index, Positive
examples.prompt: Find the real fifth root of $243$.

explanation: If $b^n = a$, then $b$ is an [[kw:nth root]] of $a$. Written as $\sqrt[n]{a}$ or $a^{1/n}$.
The integer $n$ (greater than 1) is the [[kw:index]] of the radical.
When $n$ is even and $a>0$, there are two real nth roots: $\pm \sqrt[n]{a}$. When $a<0$, there are no real nth roots.
When $n$ is odd, there is exactly one real nth root for any real $a$. For $a<0$, the root is negative.
The principal root is the positive root when $n$ is even. For odd $n$, it's the unique real root.

blocks.title: Rational Exponents and Radical Form

visuals.title: Converting Between Radical and Exponent Forms

explanation: An nth root can be written as a [[kw:rational exponent]]: $$ \sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n} $$
For any positive integer $m$: $$ a^{m/n} = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m = \sqrt[n]{a^m} $$
A negative rational exponent indicates a reciprocal: $$ a^{-m/n} = \frac{1}{a^{m/n}} $$
You can evaluate by taking the root first, then the power, or vice versa – whichever is easier.

teacherCues: Write $\sqrt{a} = a^{1/2}$ and $\sqrt[3]{a} = a^{1/3}$. Ask: What do you think $a^{m/n}$ means?

confusionCorner.title: Parentheses Matter!
confusionCorner.body: When typing into a calculator, $9^{1/5}$ must be entered as 9^(1/5). Without parentheses, 9^1/5 = 1.8, which is [[imp:wrong]]. Always enclose the exponent in parentheses.

blocks.title: Solving Equations Using nth Roots

explanation: To solve $u^n = d$, where $u$ is an algebraic expression and $n$ is an integer $>1$, take the [[kw:nth root]] of both sides.
If $n$ is odd: $u = \sqrt[n]{d}$ (one real solution).
If $n$ is even and $d \ge 0$: $u = \pm \sqrt[n]{d}$ (two real solutions if $d>0$; one if $d=0$). If $d<0$, no real solutions.
After taking the root, isolate the variable and simplify. Use a calculator to approximate if needed.

formulaCard.formula: $$ u^n = d \implies u = \begin{cases} \sqrt[n]{d}, & n \text{ odd} \\ \pm \sqrt[n]{d}, & n \text{ even}, d \ge 0 \end{cases} $$

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the $\pm$ for Even Roots
confusionCorner.body: When $n$ is even and $d>0$, $u^n = d$ has [[imp:two real solutions]]. Write $\pm \sqrt[n]{d}$. Many students forget the negative root and lose a solution.

discoveryHook.scenario: Businesses use nth roots to calculate depreciation rates. Knowing how to manipulate roots and rational exponents lets you compute the annual loss in value of equipment—a real-world algebra skill!

examples.title: Example A — Depreciation Rate
examples.prompt: An ultrasound machine costs $C = 50{,}000$, salvage value $S = 8{,}000$, life $n = 10$ years. Find $r$.

steps: The declining balance method applies a constant rate each year to the remaining value, not the original cost.
Solving for $r$ gives $r = 1 - (S/C)^{1/n}$, which uses an nth root because of the exponent $n$.
Simple division wouldn't capture the compounding effect.
examples.prompt: Why does the depreciation formula use the nth root rather than division by n?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Discuss with a partner: If you simply divided the loss by the number of years, would the annual rate be constant? How does the nth root account for compounding?
examples.title: Example B — Why nth Root?
Example C — Adjusting Salvage Value
examples.prompt: If the salvage value drops to $S = 6000$, find the new rate $r$ (same $C$, $n$).

explanation: Many real‑life formulas involve nth roots, such as the declining balance depreciation formula: $$ r = 1 - \left( \frac{S}{C} \right)^{1/n} $$
Here $C$ is original cost, $S$ is salvage value after $n$ years, $r$ is the annual depreciation rate (as a decimal).
Plug in the known values, simplify the fraction inside the parentheses, then raise to the $1/n$ power (take the nth root).
Finally, subtract from 1 to find $r$, and convert to a percentage if needed.

confusionCorner.title: Calculator Precision
confusionCorner.body: When computing $(S/C)^{1/n}$, use parentheses carefully: (S/C)^(1/n). Round only at the end to avoid cumulative errors. [[imp:Use enough decimal places]] for accurate results.

teacherCues: Show the depreciation formula $r = 1 - (S/C)^{1/n}$. Ask: What does each variable represent?

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the equation type ($u^n = d$) or formula. Note the given values and what you must solve for.
[[imp:Solve]]: If it's a simple power equation, isolate $u^n$, then take the nth root. Remember $\pm$ for even $n$. If it's a formula, substitute known values and simplify using rational exponents.

confusionCorner.body: A depreciation rate must be between 0 and 1. If you get a negative or a number >1, you've made an error. [[imp:Always check that the rate makes sense.]]
